claim: Multiple lines of evidence indicate that red blood cells are increased during cavefish development.
source: These results provide multiple lines of evidence indicating that red blood cells are increased during cavefish development.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the various experimental approaches described.

claim: hbb2 was expressed in the intermediate cell mass of the PLM during primitive hematopoiesis in Astyanax surface fish and cavefish embryos, as in zebrafish.
source: As in zebrafish (Brownlie et al., 2003; Wei et al., 2008), hbb2 was expressed in the intermediate cell mass of the PLM during primitive hematopoiesis in Astyanax surface fish and cavefish embryos (Figure 3A).

claim: In zebrafish, erythropoiesis occurs exclusively in the PLM.
source: In striking contrast to zebrafish, in which erythropoiesis occurs exclusively in the PLM, hbb2 expression was detected in both the ALM and PLM of Astyanax surface fish and cavefish embryos (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about zebrafish development supported by citations.

claim: hbb2 expression was detected in both the ALM and PLM of Astyanax surface fish and cavefish embryos.
source: In striking contrast to zebrafish, in which erythropoiesis occurs exclusively in the PLM, hbb2 expression was detected in both the ALM and PLM of Astyanax surface fish and cavefish embryos (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: gfi1aa expression was present in the ALM and PLM during Astyanax embryogenesis.
source: The expression of gfi1aa was also present in the ALM and PLM during Astyanax embryogenesis (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: gfi1aa and hbb2 staining were stronger in the cavefish ALM and PLM compared to surface fish.
source: Furthermore, gfi1aa and hbb2 staining were stronger in the cavefish ALM and PLM compared to surface fish (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: lmo2 expression confirms blood cell development in both the ALM and PLM in Astyanax embryos.
source: To further evaluate the primitive erythropoietic domains, we examined expression of the lim domain only 2 (lmo2) gene, a marker of developing blood cells (Patterson et al., 2007), by in situ hybridization. The results confirmed blood cell development in both the ALM and PLM in Astyanax embryos and revealed that both primitive erythropoietic domains are expanded in cavefish embryos (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Both primitive erythropoietic domains are expanded in cavefish embryos.
source: To further evaluate the primitive erythropoietic domains, we examined expression of the lim domain only 2 (lmo2) gene, a marker of developing blood cells (Patterson et al., 2007), by in situ hybridization. The results confirmed blood cell development in both the ALM and PLM in Astyanax embryos and revealed that both primitive erythropoietic domains are expanded in cavefish embryos (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data showing expanded lmo2 expression in Figure 3C.

claim: In zebrafish, the ALM undergoes myelopoiesis, rather than erythropoiesis, producing macrophages that disperse throughout the embryo.
source: In zebrafish, the ALM undergoes myelopoiesis, rather than erythropoiesis, producing macrophages that disperse throughout the embryo (Herbomel et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Herbomel et al., 1999.

claim: lcp1 expressing cells were distributed throughout the ventral body and yolk masses of surface fish and cavefish embryos.
source: In situ hybridization showed that lcp1 expressing cells were distributed throughout the ventral body and yolk masses of surface fish and cavefish embryos, implying that macrophages migrated from the ALM and differentiated (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Macrophages migrated from the ALM and differentiated in Astyanax embryos.
source: In situ hybridization showed that lcp1 expressing cells were distributed throughout the ventral body and yolk masses of surface fish and cavefish embryos, implying that macrophages migrated from the ALM and differentiated (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the distribution of lcp1 expressing cells shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Macrophage development does not appear to be compromised by the expansion of erythropoiesis into the ALM.
source: Therefore, macrophage development does not appear to be compromised by the expansion of erythropoiesis into the ALM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of normal lcp1 expression patterns.

claim: There is a novel domain of primitive erythropoiesis in the anterior region of Astyanax embryos.
source: In summary, the results reveal the presence of a novel domain of primitive erythropoiesis in the anterior region of Astyanax embryos and suggest that red blood cells are increased in cavefish due to expansion of both the anterior and posterior primitive erythropoiesis domains.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in situ hybridization data showing hbb2 and gfi1aa expression in the ALM.

claim: Red blood cells are increased in cavefish due to expansion of both the anterior and posterior primitive erythropoiesis domains.
source: In summary, the results reveal the presence of a novel domain of primitive erythropoiesis in the anterior region of Astyanax embryos and suggest that red blood cells are increased in cavefish due to expansion of both the anterior and posterior primitive erythropoiesis domains.

claim: Hematopoietic domains develop in the lateral mesoderm of zebrafish embryos during gastrulation.
source: Hematopoietic domains develop in the lateral mesoderm of zebrafish embryos during gastrulation (Kimmel et al., 1990), and changes in gastrulation and axis determination are under maternal control in cavefish (Ma et al., 2018; Torres-Paz et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kimmel et al., 1990.

claim: Changes in gastrulation and axis determination are under maternal control in cavefish.
source: Hematopoietic domains develop in the lateral mesoderm of zebrafish embryos during gastrulation (Kimmel et al., 1990), and changes in gastrulation and axis determination are under maternal control in cavefish (Ma et al., 2018; Torres-Paz et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ma et al., 2018 and Torres-Paz et al., 2019.

claim: The F1 hybrid progeny of the cavefish female x surface fish male cross developed more blood cells than the progeny of surface fish female x cavefish male cross.
source: The F1 hybrid progeny of the cavefish female x surface fish male and the cavefish x cavefish crosses (Figure 4C and D) developed more blood cells than the progeny of surface fish female x cavefish male and surface fish x surface fish crosses (Figure 4A and B), showing that the extent of erythrocyte development is dependent on the source of eggs.

claim: The extent of erythrocyte development is dependent on the source of eggs.

claim: The increase in cavefish blood cells is a maternally controlled trait.
source: These results reveal that the increase in cavefish blood cells is a maternally controlled trait.

claim: Erythrocytes develop early in zebrafish embryogenesis but are not required for oxygen delivery until much later in development.
source: Erythrocytes also develop early in zebrafish embryogenesis, but are not required for oxygen delivery until much later in development (Pelster and Burggren, 1996).

claim: Growth decreased in concert with hemoglobin transcript and erythrocyte reduction in surface fish.

claim: No effects on growth were seen in PHZ-treated cavefish.
source: The results also showed that growth decreased in concert with hemoglobin transcript and erythrocyte reduction in surface fish, and concordant with more red blood cells, no effects on growth were seen in PHZ-treated cavefish (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by tail length data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PHZ-treated embryos developed axial defects, most notably edemas, twisted notochords, and shortened and ventrally bent tails.

evidence: This is supported by images shown in Figure 5C and data in Table 1.

claim: Axial defects were more prevalent at lower PHZ concentrations in surface fish than cavefish embryos.
source: The PHZ-treated embryos developed axial defects, most notably edemas, twisted notochords, and shortened and ventrally bent tails (Figure 5C), which were more prevalent at lower PHZ concentrations in surface fish than cavefish embryos (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: Post-anal tail growth was significantly reduced in surface fish exposed to PHZ that virtually abolished red blood cells.

evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Notochord defects were not detected in surface fish exposed to high PHZ concentrations at 36 hpf.
source: Under these conditions, post-anal tail growth was significantly reduced, but notochord defects were not detected, suggesting that hemolytic effects on axial growth are related to the absence of red blood cells.
evidence: This is supported by observations described in the text and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Hemolytic effects on axial growth are related to the absence of red blood cells.
source: Under these conditions, post-anal tail growth was significantly reduced, but notochord defects were not detected, suggesting that hemolytic effects on axial growth are related to the absence of red blood cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that growth was reduced without notochord defects.

claim: Erythrocytes are required during early development in Astyanax.
source: The results show that erythrocytes are required during early development in Astyanax and more red blood cells may reduce the sensitivity of cavefish to hemolytic anemia.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the PHZ experiments showing developmental effects.

claim: More red blood cells may reduce the sensitivity of cavefish to hemolytic anemia.
source: The results show that erythrocytes are required during early development in Astyanax and more red blood cells may reduce the sensitivity of cavefish to hemolytic anemia.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the differential effects of PHZ on surface fish and cavefish.

claim: Subterranean waters harboring Astyanax cavefish are low in oxygen.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Rohner et al., 2013; Ornelas-García et al., 2018; Boggs and Gross, 2021.

claim: Oxygen is essential for normal development and growth.
source: Subterranean waters harboring Astyanax cavefish are low in oxygen (Rohner et al., 2013; Ornelas-García et al., 2018; Boggs and Gross, 2021), which is essential for normal development and growth (Giaccia et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Giaccia et al., 2004.

source: The results showed that hypoxia reduced the number of red blood cells in the DC and suppressed growth in surface fish but not cavefish (Figure 6B), showing that cavefish are more resistant to oxygen depletion.

claim: Hypoxia suppressed growth in surface fish but not cavefish.
source: The results showed that hypoxia reduced the number of red blood cells in the DC and suppressed growth in surface fish but not cavefish (Figure 6B), showing that cavefish are more resistant to oxygen depletion.

claim: Cavefish are more resistant to oxygen depletion than surface fish.
source: The results showed that hypoxia reduced the number of red blood cells in the DC and suppressed growth in surface fish but not cavefish (Figure 6B), showing that cavefish are more resistant to oxygen depletion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of hypoxia on growth shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Eye growth is especially sensitive to hypoxia because of the energy cost associated with retinal differentiation and maintenance.
source: Reasoning that eye growth would be especially sensitive to hypoxia because of the energy cost associated with retinal differentiation and maintenance (Wong-Riley, 2010; Moran et al., 2015), eye size was also examined in surface fish and cavefish exposed to normoxia or hypoxia for 18 hr.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wong-Riley, 2010 and Moran et al., 2015.

claim: Eye size was more sensitive to hypoxia relative to normoxia in surface fish compared to cavefish.
source: The results showed that eye size was more sensitive to hypoxia relative to normoxia in surface fish compared to cavefish (Figure 6C).

claim: Cavefish growth is resistant to hypoxia.

source: The results suggest that cavefish growth is resistant to hypoxia and development of more erythrocytes may contribute to hypoxia tolerance.

source: Exposure of surface fish or cavefish larvae to hypoxia for 2 hr. resulted in increased transcript levels of the insulin growth factor binding protein 1a (igfbp1a) gene, the HIF1 family genes hif1aa and hif1a-like2, and the HIF1-regulated downstream gene hexokinase 1 (hk1) (Figure 7).

claim: Exposure of surface fish or cavefish larvae to hypoxia for 2 hr resulted in increased transcript levels of hif1aa.
source: Exposure of surface fish or cavefish larvae to hypoxia for 2 hr. resulted in increased transcript levels of the insulin growth factor binding protein 1a (igfbp1a) gene, the HIF1 family genes hif1aa and hif1a-like2, and the HIF1-regulated downstream gene hexokinase 1 (hk1) (Figure 7).

source: Exposure of surface fish or cavefish larvae to hypoxia for 2 hr. resulted in increased transcript levels of the insulin growth factor binding protein 1a (igfbp1a) gene, the HIF1 family genes hif1aa and hif1a-like2, and the HIF1-regulated downstream gene hexokinase 1 (hk1) (Figure 7).

source: Exposure of surface fish or cavefish larvae to hypoxia for 2 hr. resulted in increased transcript levels of the insulin growth factor binding protein 1a (igfbp1a) gene, the HIF1 family genes hif1aa and hif1a-like2, and the HIF1-regulated downstream gene hexokinase 1 (hk1) (Figure 7).

source: In contrast, the hifab and hif1a-like genes were expressed at similar levels in normoxic cavefish and hypoxic surface fish (Figure 7), implying constitutive expression in cavefish.

claim: hifab and hif1a-like are constitutively expressed in cavefish.
source: In contrast, the hifab and hif1a-like genes were expressed at similar levels in normoxic cavefish and hypoxic surface fish (Figure 7), implying constitutive expression in cavefish.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that these genes are expressed at high levels in normoxic cavefish.

claim: The expression of g6pd, ldha, and pdk1 genes were not significantly increased by hypoxia in surface fish or cavefish.
source: The expression of the glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (g6pd), lactate dehydrogenase a (ldha), and pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase 1 (pdk1) genes were not significantly increased by hypoxia in surface fish or cavefish (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7.

claim: igfbp1, hif1a-like2, and hk1 are upregulated by hypoxia in both surface fish and cavefish.
source: The results indicate that igfbp1, hif1a-like2, and hk1 are upregulated by hypoxia in both surface fish and cavefish, whereas hif1aa and hif1a-like are expressed at higher levels in cavefish than in surface fish in either normoxic or hypoxic laboratory conditions.

claim: hif1aa and hif1a-like are expressed at higher levels in cavefish than in surface fish in either normoxic or hypoxic laboratory conditions.
source: The results indicate that igfbp1, hif1a-like2, and hk1 are upregulated by hypoxia in both surface fish and cavefish, whereas hif1aa and hif1a-like are expressed at higher levels in cavefish than in surface fish in either normoxic or hypoxic laboratory conditions.
evidence: This is a summary of the qPCR results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Cavefish exhibit a complex molecular response to hypoxia: some oxygen sensing genes are upregulated, others are not changed, and some genes may be insensitive to oxygen depletion because they are already expressed at maximal levels in normoxic cavefish.
source: Thus, cavefish exhibit a complex molecular response to hypoxia: some oxygen sensing genes are upregulated, others are not changed, and some of the latter genes may be insensitive to oxygen depletion because they are already expressed at maximal levels in normoxic cavefish.

claim: Cavefish embryos develop more red blood cells than surface fish embryos when raised under normoxic laboratory conditions.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Martinez et al., 2004; Timmerman and Chapman, 2004; Rutjes et al., 2007; Haase, 2013.

source: In addition, we report that the increase in erythrocytes may be caused by expansion of embryonic hematopoietic domains in cavefish compared to surface fish.

claim: Adult cavefish have more erythrocytes in their head kidneys compared to surface fish.
source: Further investigation will be required to determine whether erythrocytes are also increased in adults, although this possibility seems likely because adult cavefish have increased levels of hemoglobin transcripts (Sears et al., 2020) and more erythrocytes in their head kidneys compared to surface fish (Peuß et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Peuß et al., 2020.

claim: Cavefish have evolved a permanent enhancement in red blood cells as a potential adaptation for survival in hypoxic cave waters.

source: The results showed that surface fish and cavefish primitive erythrocytes are derived from two different hematopoietic domains, one located anteriorly in the ALM and the other posteriorly in the PLM.

claim: Expansion of the posterior hematopoietic domain can be induced in zebrafish by overexpressing LMO2 together with its partner transcription factor SCL/TAL1.
source: It is noteworthy that expansion of the posterior hematopoietic domain can also be induced in zebrafish by overexpressing LMO2 together with its partner transcription factor SCL/TAL1 (Gering et al., 2003), suggesting that teleosts have the capacity to modulate blood cell numbers by changing the size of primitive erythropoietic domains during development.

claim: Teleosts have the capacity to modulate blood cell numbers by changing the size of primitive erythropoietic domains during development.
source: It is noteworthy that expansion of the posterior hematopoietic domain can also be induced in zebrafish by overexpressing LMO2 together with its partner transcription factor SCL/TAL1 (Gering et al., 2003), suggesting that teleosts have the capacity to modulate blood cell numbers by changing the size of primitive erythropoietic domains during development.

claim: The existence of erythrocyte forming capacity in the ALM of surface fish suggests that the expansion of primitive erythropoiesis may pre-adapt Astyanax for colonizing hypoxic cave environments.

claim: The expansion of erythropoiesis into the ALM during primitive hematopoiesis in Astyanax contrasts strikingly to zebrafish, medaka, and other teleosts.
source: The expansion of erythropoiesis into the ALM during primitive hematopoiesis in Astyanax contrasts strikingly to zebrafish, medaka, and other teleosts that have been investigated, in which primitive erythropoiesis is confined to the PLM, and the ALM is devoted only to myelopoiesis (Detrich et al., 1995; Govoni et al., 2005; Moriyama et al., 2010).

claim: In zebrafish, medaka, and other teleosts, primitive erythropoiesis is confined to the PLM, and the ALM is devoted only to myelopoiesis.
source: The expansion of erythropoiesis into the ALM during primitive hematopoiesis in Astyanax contrasts strikingly to zebrafish, medaka, and other teleosts that have been investigated, in which primitive erythropoiesis is confined to the PLM, and the ALM is devoted only to myelopoiesis (Detrich et al., 1995; Govoni et al., 2005; Moriyama et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Detrich et al., 1995; Govoni et al., 2005; Moriyama et al., 2010.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Ren et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2018; Torres-Paz et al., 2019.
